tldr: Existing 3D reconstruction models suffer from arbitrary scale shifts across viewpoints and input setups. MAGP solves this by accurately recovering absolute metric scales (in meters) from camera motion and depth. Seamlessly plugged into robot policies, it slashes absolute error while boosting manipulation success rates by up to 6.26%.
hero_caption: Comparison between conventional relative geometry (left) and our metric geometry (right). Under relative geometry, the predicted cushion length fluctuates widely between 0.48m and 1.2m across viewpoints, failing physical alignment. In contrast, metric geometry consistently preserves the true 0.6m scale regardless of the viewing angle.
overview:
Recent foundation models for robotics increasingly incorporate 3D representations (point clouds and depth) to improve spatial reasoning and dexterous manipulation. However, existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction models, such as DUSt3R and Depth Anything 3, rely on per-scene normalization and only recover "relative geometry." As a result, predicted object dimensions and distances shift wildly whenever viewpoints or input order change, creating a fundamental mismatch with real-world robot actions defined in metric units like millimeters and meters.

To bridge this gap, the authors propose Metric-Aware Geometry Perception (MAGP), an end-to-end framework that outputs real-scale geometric tokens and plugs directly into existing robotic policies. Its core innovation is Metric Scale Equivariant Augmentation (MSEA), which prevents the model from guessing scale based on appearance (visual priors such as object categories and room layout). By physically rescaling only observation values—like camera translation and depth—MSEA trains the model to strictly follow observed numbers and output metric geometry. In addition, a flexible conditioning mechanism accommodates heterogeneous robotic setups where camera parameters and depth sensors vary in presence and density.

In experiments on 3D reconstruction benchmarks such as ETH3D and ScanNet++, MAGP drastically reduces absolute error from 2.01m down to 0.07m. Furthermore, integrating MAGP into robot manipulation benchmarks like LIBERO and RoboTwin yields up to a 6.26% success rate gain on RoboTwin, while also substantially strengthening zero-shot robustness in novel, perturbed environments.
contributions: Proposed MAGP, the first plug-and-play, end-to-end metric geometry perception framework that aligns 3D reconstruction directly with physical robot actions on a shared real-world scale.

Designed Metric Scale Equivariant Augmentation (MSEA) to derive physical scale directly from camera motion and depth without relying on visual priors, paired with a flexible input conditioning scheme robust to missing or sparse data.
Reduced absolute 3D reconstruction error by over an order of magnitude, from 2.01m to 0.07m, while simultaneously improving relative geometric accuracy.
Consistently boosted policy manipulation success rates across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and the perturbed zero-shot benchmark LIBERO-Plus.

sections.heading: Right Shape, Wrong Size? Why Relative Geometry Confuses Robots
sections.summary: While recent 3D reconstruction techniques are increasingly used in robotics, existing feed-forward methods only capture normalized relative geometry, causing object sizes and distances to drift across viewpoints. Because these scale discrepancies degrade end-effector control, this work introduces MAGP to feed scale-consistent metric representations directly into policies.
sections.details:
For a robot to grasp objects and manipulate them precisely, 2D semantic information is not enough—explicit 3D geometric information is essential. Recent advances in feed-forward 3D reconstruction models have prompted many researchers to feed point clouds and depth maps directly into robot policies.

However, there is a catch. Under perspective projection, identical images can be produced by objects of different physical sizes placed at different distances from the camera. As a result, existing reconstruction models normalize scale per scene, recovering only "relative geometry." While relative geometry accurately reproduces overall shape and spatial layout, it lacks an absolute physical reference. Consequently, changing the camera viewpoint causes the estimated length of the exact same cushion to drift unpredictably between 0.48m and 1.2m.

Under such inconsistency, a robot cannot determine how many centimeters to move its end-effector. The same action command results in completely different physical displacements depending on the camera angle, making accurate manipulation impossible. What robots truly require is "metric geometry" anchored to a shared physical scale in meters across all observations.

Yet, learning metric geometry is non-trivial. Instead of computing scale from physical cues such as camera translation and depth readings, models easily fall back on "visual priors"—guessing scale from object appearance or room composition. MAGP resolves this issue, providing a plug-and-play architecture that supplies metric geometry tokens directly to downstream policies.

captions.F1: Comparison of geometric reconstruction across viewpoints. On the left (relative geometry), predicted cushion dimensions vary wildly across viewpoints (0.48m, 1.2m, 0.54m), causing alignment failures in a shared coordinate frame. On the right (metric geometry), the actual 0.6m dimension is preserved consistently across all views, enabling seamless integration.

sections.heading: From Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction to Robot Geometry Perception
sections.summary: 3D reconstruction has evolved into fast, one-shot feed-forward models like DUSt3R and Depth Anything 3, but these still rely on relative scales. Meanwhile, robotic policies are adopting 3D geometry, yet none have fully grounded their representations in true metric dimensions.
sections.details:
This section organizes related prior work into two main threads:

- Advances in 3D Geometric Reconstruction
Moving away from slow optimization-based pipelines, recent efforts have shifted to feed-forward models like DUSt3R and MASt3R that directly perform pairwise point regression and matching. Subsequent architectures such as VGGT, CUT3R, and $\pi^{3}$ extended this to multi-view setups, followed by Depth Anything 3 (DA3), MapAnything, and large-scale scaling efforts like VGGT-$\Omega$. Nevertheless, these models prioritize visual shape fidelity and rely on per-scene normalization, leaving real-world scale recovery unaddressed.

- Geometry-Conditioned Robotic Manipulation
In robotics, approaches such as 3DS-VLA, DepthVLA, VGGT-DP, and ABot-M0 have explored injecting 3D point clouds, depth maps, or pretrained geometric representations into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. While these methods demonstrate improved manipulation accuracy, the geometry they consume remains strictly relative. MAGP sets itself apart by directly outputting metric-aware geometric tokens and feeding them into downstream policies.

sections.heading: Why Do Models Ignore Physical Scale and Get Fooled by Appearance?
sections.summary: Analyzing the formulation of relative geometry reveals why models ignore camera translation and depth, relying instead on visual appearance to guess scale. To overcome this limitation, the authors formally introduce the requirement of Metric Scale Equivariance.
sections.details:
When reconstructing a 3D point cloud from multi-view images $\mathcal{I} = \{I_i\}_{i=1}^N$, one can unproject pixels into a true-scale point cloud $\mathcal{P}$ given camera intrinsics $K_i$, extrinsics $[R_i | t_i]$, and depth $D_i$.

However, existing models $\phi_\theta(\cdot)$ normalize both predictions and ground truth per scene using $\mathcal{N}(\cdot)$ to bypass scale ambiguity, optimizing with a relative geometry loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}$. Because $\mathcal{N}(s\mathcal{P}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathcal{P})$ holds for any constant $s > 0$, the model is content predicting $\hat{\mathcal{P}} = s\mathcal{P}$ with an unknown scale factor $s$. This tells a robot where to reach in relative space, but not how many physical centimeters it must move to get there.

Can this be fixed simply by removing normalization and regressing the point cloud directly using a physical metric loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{metric}}$? In practice, no. Experiments show that models quickly learn to ignore physical numeric cues—such as camera translation $t$ and depth $\mathcal{D}$—and instead guess scale directly from visual appearance ($s \sim \phi_\theta(\mathcal{I})$), relying on visual priors like apparent object sizes and furniture layouts.

To counter this shortcut, the authors introduce the property of "Metric Scale Equivariance." When input camera translations and depth observations are scaled by a factor $\alpha$, the reconstructed 3D space must also scale by exactly $\alpha$ ($\phi_\theta(\mathcal{I}, \alpha t, \alpha\mathcal{D}) = \alpha \phi_\theta(\mathcal{I}, t, \mathcal{D})$). Enforcing this physical constraint during training is crucial.

captions.F2: For the same set of images, doubling camera translation and depth observations means the physical scene is twice as large. Scale-equivariant reconstruction (middle row) tracks the changes in physical observations and correctly scales up by 2x (e.g., 1.19m to 2.38m). In contrast, the standard model without equivariance (bottom row) is biased by visual appearance, remaining stuck around 1.17m.

sections.heading: Inside MAGP: A Unified Transformer and Cheat-Proof Training
sections.summary: MAGP transforms multi-view images, camera parameters, and depth maps into geometric tokens using a single Transformer, fusing them with visual-language features via residual cross-attention. It is trained with Metric Scale Equivariant Augmentation (MSEA) and sensor-robust conditioning.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Architectural Design
MAGP employs a clean, end-to-end design based on a single Transformer backbone.

- Metric-Aware Geometry Modeling
For each view, image patch tokens are concatenated with camera tokens embedded via a lightweight MLP (when available) and added to patch-embedded depth tokens. Missing observations are replaced with learnable placeholder tokens. Alternating intra-view self-attention in shallow layers with cross-view attention in deeper layers allows the model to process arbitrary view counts without requiring a separate fusion module. The decoder (a DPT head and camera head) outputs absolute-scale depth maps and camera poses.

- Metric to Action Grounding
The extracted geometric tokens $\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{geo}}$ are fused with visual-language features $\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{vl}}$ from a VLM backbone (Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct) via residual cross-attention. By setting $\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{vl}}$ as queries and geometric tokens as keys/values, metric-scale geometry is injected directly into action predictions without compromising the VLM's language understanding.

### 4.2 Robust Optimization for Metric Geometry
Several techniques prevent the model from exploiting visual shortcuts and make it resilient to heterogeneous sensor setups.

- Metric Scale Equivariant Augmentation (MSEA)
During training, images remain unchanged while camera translations, input depth maps, and ground-truth point clouds are rescaled by a random factor $\alpha$. Forcing identical images to map to different physical scales compels the model to rely on camera parameters and depth rather than visual heuristics.

- Flexible Metric Conditioning
On real robots, camera poses or depth data may be available for only a subset of views, or depth may be sparse. To handle this, camera and depth inputs are randomly dropped per view during training, and spatial masks are applied to depth maps to vary sparsity. This ensures smooth operation across arbitrary sensor combinations.

- Hybrid Relative and Absolute Loss
The training objective combines a relative geometry loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ to preserve fine shape details with a metric loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{metric}}$ to anchor physical scale: $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}} + m_{\mathrm{metric}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{metric}}$. When metric observations are completely absent, $m_{\mathrm{metric}}=0$, allowing stable training solely on relative geometry.

captions.F3: Overall architecture of MAGP: (1) Inputs include multiple images with optional camera poses and depth maps. (2) A unified Transformer extracts metric geometry tokens. (3) These tokens are fused with VLM backbone features via residual cross-attention. (4) An Action Expert using Flow Matching predicts precise end-effector actions grounded in physical dimensions.

sections.heading: Absolute Error Drops from 2m to 7cm, Boosting Robot Success Rates
sections.summary: MAGP drastically reduces absolute error on 3D reconstruction benchmarks (ETH3D, MegaDepth, ScanNet++) while consistently improving manipulation success across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and LIBERO-Plus. Ablation studies confirm the critical role of MSEA and hybrid loss design.
sections.details:
### 5.1 3D Reconstruction Evaluation
MAGP was evaluated across three benchmarks: ETH3D, MegaDepth, and ScanNet++, using relative inlier ratios ($\delta_{1.03}$, $\delta_{1.25}$) and absolute error in meters (Abs).

- Comparison with Baselines
Even in an image-only setup, MAGP outperforms DA3 in depth inlier ratio by +17.41% (74.23% vs. 56.82%). Its full potential is unlocked when camera parameters and depth are provided: in the fully conditioned setting, absolute error drops to 0.11m for depth and 0.06m for point clouds. Compared to baseline absolute errors exceeding 2m, this represents an improvement of over an order of magnitude.

- Ablation Experiments
Removing MSEA causes scale-tracking ability to collapse as the model falls back on appearance priors (Table 2). In loss function ablations, training with $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{metric}}$ alone degrades fine shape fidelity; combining it with relative loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ is necessary to achieve both crisp geometric details and accurate physical scale (Table 3). A normalization factor of $\mu=10$, aligning well with robotic workspaces, delivered the best results.

### 5.2 Robot Manipulation Evaluation
- LIBERO & RoboTwin
On LIBERO, adding MAGP improves StarVLA-$\pi$ success rate from 96.8% to 98.1%, and GR00T from 97.5% to 98.5%. On RoboTwin, which features challenging bimanual manipulation, GR00T's average success rate surges from 81.69% to 87.95% (+6.26%), while DM0.5 improves from 92.12% to 93.91%.

- Zero-Shot Robustness on LIBERO-Plus
Under heavy disturbances in LIBERO-Plus, GR00T+MAGP achieves an 80.3% success rate, outperforming the baseline by 3.9% and the relative geometry model by 1.3%. Under perturbations to initial robot states, the success rate jumps from 49.0% to 63.9% (nearly a 15% boost), demonstrating that accurate physical scale perception directly reinforces robustness to proprioceptive shifts.

captions.F4: Point clouds reconstructed independently from three separate subsets and merged together. MAGP (top) achieves perfect scale alignment across subsets, resulting in clean, seamless integration. In contrast, DA3 (bottom) exhibits inconsistent scales across subsets, leading to double vision and severe geometric collapse upon fusion.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Restoring Real-World Physical Scale to Robot Perception
sections.summary: MAGP offers an end-to-end framework connecting geometric reconstruction and robotic action prediction on a unified physical scale. Its effectiveness across 3D reconstruction and robot manipulation marks an important stepping stone toward future foundation models for robotics.
sections.details:
This work proposed MAGP to overcome the relative-scale limitation that plagues existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. By pairing Metric Scale Equivariant Augmentation with flexible metric conditioning, the framework removes visual bias and consistently perceives metric physical scale in meters using camera motion and depth.

The dramatic reduction in absolute 3D error, alongside consistent performance gains and disturbance robustness across robot manipulation benchmarks, highlights the indispensable role of accurate real-world scale in robotic perception.

sections.heading: Appendix: Training Details, Low Overhead, and Qualitative Visuals
sections.summary: Built on DA3-Giant and trained across 32 H100 GPUs using a two-stage view curriculum, MAGP adds only 0.001B parameters and 2ms of latency. It delivers highly accurate point cloud reconstructions and robust policy execution across diverse indoor and outdoor scenes.
sections.details:
The appendix provides implementation details, computational overhead analysis, and visual qualitative results.

- Training Setup and Computational Overhead
Training utilizes diverse synthetic and real datasets, including UnrealStereo4K and ScanNet++. Leveraging 32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, a two-stage curriculum scales view counts from 2–4 views up to 2–18 views. Despite its capabilities, MAGP adds only 0.001B parameters (approx. 1 million) over DA3-Giant for the depth patch embedding layer. On an NVIDIA A800 GPU, inference latency increases by a mere 2ms (from 152ms to 154ms), imposing virtually no runtime burden for real-world deployment.

- Depth Generation and Qualitative Results in Robotics
Because benchmarks like LIBERO lack native depth and camera parameters, the pretrained monocular estimator MoGe was used to generate pseudo-depth from the head camera. In qualitative evaluations (Fig. 5), red dashed reference lines representing identical physical lengths align perfectly between ground truth (GT) and prediction (PR) across diverse indoor and outdoor scenes, confirming accurate metric reconstruction without any post-hoc scale alignment.

captions.F5: Qualitative results of metric geometry reconstruction with MAGP. Red dashed lines of identical length are drawn between GT and PR. Dimensions of furniture, vehicles, and rooms align precisely across indoor and outdoor scenes without post-hoc scale adjustments.
captions.F7: Execution rollouts on RoboTwin under clean and randomized environments. Even when initial object locations, lighting, and background textures change significantly, metric geometry maintains stable spatial grounding, allowing tasks like grasping and hammering to succeed reliably.

takeaways: When providing 3D geometric features to robot policies, providing true metric scale rather than relative shape directly enhances physical action accuracy.

Metric Scale Equivariant Augmentation (MSEA)—scaling physical parameters while keeping visual appearance fixed—is highly effective at forcing models to rely on physical cues over appearance heuristics.
Multi-task optimization combining relative loss (preserving structural detail) and metric loss (guaranteeing physical scale) is essential to achieve both visual fidelity and scale accuracy.
MAGP introduces minimal overhead over base reconstruction models (+0.001B parameters, +2ms latency), making it easy to plug into existing VLA policies.
limitations: In robot benchmark evaluations (e.g., LIBERO), true sensor depth is unavailable, so pseudo-depth from a monocular estimator (MoGe) was used; behavior may differ when using raw sensor depth.
When camera motion is minimal or depth cues are entirely absent, absolute scale recovery accuracy degrades toward that of relative geometry models.
Evaluations focused primarily on simulated benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin); large-scale validation under the severe sensor noise and calibration drift of real-world robot hardware remains future work.
